lines.text: "Wait quietly"-this attitude however must be manifested
in the quite concrete circumstances of our daily life, and
precisely now in the crisis through which we are passing. We
stand amid the ruins of a world that has collapsed, and we
have to build it afresh. Not only is the outer structure of
our world shattered—our cities and houses, our resources for
trade and production, but the spiritual capital on which
a people must live has also been swept away and annihilated:
morals, the consciousness of right, and the rule of right itself.
Everyone who is called to co-operate in some degree (and to
a certain extent we are all so called) realizes what heavy work
lies before us. It is work which brooks no delay; but amid all
the energy required, and the urgent haste to put our hands to
the plough, there is one thing of which we must again and
again sharply remind ourselves. Patience is necessary! not
patience in regard to our duties, but patience and inner calm
regarding our expectations. Not patience as concerns what we
have to demand of ourselves, but patience about what we
demand of the future.
When here in Marburg a few weeks ago Professor Franz
Bohm gave a lecture on the decline of law and right in the
Third Reich, and in conclusion turned his thoughts to the
future that is to emerge, he ended with the warning:
"Have patience!" When in Whitsuntide week foreign
experts met German professors to discuss together the crushing
problems of international trade we had to listen to the
repeated warning issued by foreign friends that we must
exercise patience. Too much has happened, too much has
been shattered and laid in ruins for our world to be put right
again at one stroke and as if the terror through which we
have passed had not taken place.
An old tag runs: "A heavy load of impatient zeal is not so
powertul as to counterbalance a dram of dire misfortune."
And not only is impatience useless but actually mischievous,
harming ourselves who are so impatient, who in the illusions
we foster can only be dooming ourselves to disappointment;
who then, dismayed and in a mood of hopeless resignation,
will lose all courage and will no longer wish to co-operate
